role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: The outside view: forecasting from reference classes
summary: Your own estimate of cost and time is built from the inside, from the plan in front of you, and it is reliably optimistic. The outside view starts instead from what actually happened on a class of similar projects, then adjusts. That habit is the single strongest defence against the planning fallacy.
body:
Every estimate you make from your own plan, step by step, is the inside view, and it is reliably optimistic. The outside view starts from what actually happened on a group of similar projects, and only then adjusts for what is genuinely different about yours. Start outside, then step in.

Recall

Q. In lesson 4, why should a schedule treat a public approval as a risk rather than a date?

A. Because the authority having jurisdiction controls the criteria and the timing; approvals can be delayed, conditioned or appealed.

Q. In lesson 1, when is uncertainty highest in the lifecycle?

A. At the start, when the least money is committed, which is why early money buys the most information.

Q. In lesson 5, what was the weakest number in the expected value calculation?

A. The probability, because it is a judgment; you must ask where it came from.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, every number in a development pro forma is a forecast, and the forecasts that hurt most are cost and time. Lesson 1 showed that a 10 percent overrun can remove 70 percent of a profit. If your estimates are systematically optimistic, you are not occasionally unlucky; you are systematically losing. This week is about judgment, and the first tool of judgment is knowing where your own forecasts come from.

Inside view and outside view

In plain English: the inside view looks at your project. You list the tasks, estimate each one and add them up. It feels rigorous because it is detailed. The outside view ignores the details at first and asks a blunter question: when people did projects like this before, how long did they take and what did they cost, compared with what they planned?

The psychologist Daniel Kahneman, who developed these ideas with Amos Tversky, tells a story against himself in his book Thinking, Fast and Slow. He and colleagues were writing a school curriculum, and the team estimated it would take about two years. He then asked one member, an experienced curriculum developer, how long similar teams had taken. The answer, by Kahneman's account, was that a substantial share never finished, and those that did took around seven to ten years. The team carried on anyway. The project took about eight years. The expert had the outside view in his head the whole time, and nobody, including him, had used it.

The professional framing has a name for the bias: the planning fallacy, which is the tendency to underestimate the time, cost and risk of a planned action while overestimating its benefits, even when you know similar projects ran over. The inside view produces it because a plan describes what will happen if things go as planned, and things rarely do. The overruns come from events you did not list: a late permit, a trade going bust, a wet winter, a design change. You cannot list them in advance, but the reference class has already experienced them.

Reference class forecasting, step by step

A reference class is a group of past projects similar enough to yours that their outcomes tell you something about yours. Reference class forecasting, a method developed by the planner Bent Flyvbjerg building on Kahneman's work, runs in three steps.

  1. Choose the reference class: projects of the same type, similar scale, similar delivery method and, where possible, similar market.
  2. Get the distribution of outcomes: not just the average, but how often and by how much those projects ran over budget and schedule.
  3. Place your project in that distribution, and adjust only for differences you can actually evidence.

Worked example one. This is hypothetical. Your inside-view schedule for a 40-unit wood-frame apartment building, from permit to occupancy, is 18 months. You gather 12 comparable buildings completed in your region over recent years, from permit records, contractors and other owners. Their actual durations, permit to occupancy, have a middle value of 23 months, and three of the 12 took more than 27 months.

Your plan sits below every one of them. That does not prove your 18 months is wrong, but it shifts the burden of proof onto you. Before you rely on 18, you must explain in writing what makes your project faster than all twelve. "Our contractor is good" is not an explanation; every owner said that. "The building is repeated from a completed design already approved by the same building department" might be.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example two: cost

Still hypothetical. Your cost consultant's estimate for the same building is $12 million. From the same 12 projects you learn how far final cost exceeded the budget at the same stage of design. Suppose the middle overrun was 8 percent and roughly one project in five ran over by 18 percent or more.

The outside view says: on a $12 million estimate, a typical outcome is about $12.96 million, and a bad but not unusual outcome is about $14.16 million. Now go back to lesson 3. If your profit on cost cushion is 14 percent, an 18 percent overrun eats all of it. The reference class has just told you that losing your entire profit is roughly a one-in-five event on this kind of project. That is a decision-changing fact, and it came from other people's experience, not from your plan.

Two cautions. A reference class that is too narrow, three projects by one builder, gives you noise. One that is too broad, every building ever built, tells you nothing about yours. Aim for the middle, and say which projects you chose and why. And beware of selecting the class to get the answer you want: a reference class assembled after you already like the deal is the inside view wearing a disguise.

How the best do it

Some governments have written the outside view into their rules. The British government's appraisal guidance, the HM Treasury Green Book, asks appraisers of public projects to adjust their estimates for optimism bias, using adjustments drawn from evidence about how similar projects actually turned out. The idea is that an estimate is not finished until it has been corrected for the known tendency of estimates to be too low. A small developer can copy the principle with almost no cost: keep a simple spreadsheet of every project you can learn about in your market, with planned and actual cost and duration, and check every new estimate against it before it reaches a gate.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that you have no reference class at all, and so you default to the inside view without noticing. The control is to start the class now, before you need it: permit records, completion notices, conversations with contractors and lenders about how long jobs really took. Lenders and cost consultants often know the pattern; ask them directly.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes his project is the exception. Everyone does. The professional assumes he is typical until the evidence says otherwise, and writes down the evidence. A useful test: if you removed your name from the project and gave the file to a stranger with the reference class beside it, which number would the stranger believe?

Callback

In lesson 5, Roman warned that the probability is the weakest number in an expected value calculation, and promised you a better way to find it. This is that way. The 25 percent chance of a hidden site problem should come from a reference class: of the last 20 sites like this one, how many had a problem of that kind? That turns a feeling into a figure someone can check.

Recap

The inside view builds your estimate from your plan and is reliably optimistic; that is the planning fallacy. The outside view starts from a reference class of similar projects and their actual outcomes, then adjusts only for differences you can evidence. Choose the class honestly, use its distribution, and make your own estimate explain any gap.

Next: Ford, Failure Forensics — the Sydney Opera House, a date and a budget with no reference class.
checklist: Write down your inside-view estimate of cost and duration before looking at comparables.
Build a reference class of similar projects in your market, and record why each one was included.
Find the middle outcome and the bad-but-not-unusual outcome, not just the average.
Explain in writing every gap between your estimate and the reference class.
Check the reference-class overrun against your profit-on-cost cushion.
Start a planned-versus-actual record now, before you need it.
Ask lenders and cost consultants how long similar jobs actually took.
head: Field checklist
speak: My own estimate, built task by task from my plan, is the inside view, and it is reliably optimistic. That is the planning fallacy. The outside view starts with a reference class: projects like mine, and what actually happened to their cost and schedule. On a hypothetical 40-unit building, if I plan 18 months but twelve comparable buildings took a middle value of 23, the burden of proof is on me to explain, in writing, why mine is faster. On cost, if the middle overrun in the class is eight percent and one in five ran eighteen percent or more, and my profit cushion is fourteen percent, then losing the whole profit is roughly a one-in-five event. That fact changes decisions. I choose the class honestly, before I fall for the deal, and I keep a planned-versus-actual record of every project I can learn about.
terms: Inside view — an estimate built up from the details of your own plan.
Outside view — an estimate that starts from the actual outcomes of similar past projects.
Reference class — a group of past projects similar enough to yours that their outcomes inform your forecast.

hostile.q: You say eighteen months. Every builder in this town says eighteen months and takes two years. Why are you different?
hostile.a: I may not be. My reference class of twelve similar buildings has a middle of 23 months, so my financing is sized for 24 with an extension option, and my gate assumes 23. I will show you the class and the one difference I think shortens our timeline, with the evidence for it.

title: Sydney Opera House: a date and a budget with no reference class
summary: The Sydney Opera House was given an early estimate of about A$7 million and a target opening in 1963; it opened on 20 October 1973 at a reported cost of about A$102 million. Construction started before the design existed, the estimate had no reference class, and the architect left before completion. The building is a masterpiece and the project was a failure, and both are true.
body:
The Sydney Opera House is one of the great buildings of the twentieth century, and as a project it failed on cost and time by a factor no developer could survive. The estimate was an inside-view guess about a building that had not yet been designed, and construction started before anyone knew how to build the roof.

Recall

Q. In lesson 5, what is the expected value of perfect information?

A. The most it is worth paying to remove an uncertainty completely before you decide.

Q. What was Rule 1?

A. No date, announcement or sunk cost moves me past a gate. Only the gate's written criteria do.

Q. In lesson 1, which lever does the developer control most?

A. Time, because most delay begins with a decision that was not made.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this case separates two things beginners mix up: whether the building is good and whether the project succeeded. A developer is judged on both, and money is lost on the second. The public sponsor here could absorb a catastrophic overrun through a state lottery and years of patience. A private developer with the same overrun is bankrupt long before the opening night.

Step 1: Timeline

The government of New South Wales held an international design competition, and in January 1957 the Danish architect Jørn Utzon was announced as the winner, with a striking scheme of sail-like roof shells. An early cost estimate of about 7 million Australian dollars, in the currency adopted later, was attached to the project, with a target to open in early 1963. Construction of the podium began in 1959. The roof geometry took years to resolve with the engineers, Ove Arup and Partners, and some early work had to be revisited once the roof design was settled. After a change of state government in 1965, disputes over costs and payments between Utzon and the new Minister for Public Works escalated, and Utzon resigned in 1966 and left Australia. A local team completed the building, with interiors that differ from his designs. It opened on 20 October 1973. The final cost is widely reported as about 102 million Australian dollars, largely funded by a state lottery.

Step 2: Key decisions

  • Accepting an early budget and date for a building of a kind nobody had built before.
  • Starting construction before the design, and in particular the roof, was resolved.
  • Letting the relationship between the client and the architect break down mid-project, so that the person who held the design intent left before completion.

Step 3: Assumptions

The central assumption was that a competition-winning concept was close enough to a design to be estimated and scheduled. It was not. Nobody yet knew how the shells would be structured, so nobody could know what they would cost. The estimate was the inside view at its purest: a number for the plan as imagined, with no class of comparable buildings to test it against, because there was none. The honest outside-view answer would have been: "unprecedented buildings of this kind tend to overrun badly, and we cannot yet say by how much."

Step 4: Incentives

Accounts of the project describe political pressure to get construction visibly underway, so that the project would be hard for a later government to stop. Whatever the precise motives, the incentive pattern is common and worth naming: a sponsor who wants a project to happen benefits from starting early and from a low first estimate, because both make it easier to approve. The low number gets the yes; the true number arrives after it is too late to say no. Every developer meets that incentive in himself.

Say that out loud now.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The roof geometry remained unsolved while the podium was being built. Estimates were revised upward repeatedly. Work completed early had to be revisited. Each of those is a signal that the original budget and date no longer described the project. The process continued on the momentum of the start rather than on a reset estimate at a gate.

Step 6: Point of no return

The point of no return was the decision to start building before the design existed. From then on, every design decision had to fit what was already in the ground, and every delay in the design became a delay on site. Once the podium was underway, abandoning or re-scoping the project carried a political and financial cost that made continuing almost inevitable.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause was committing to a cost and a date with no reference class and no resolved design, and then starting construction before either existed. The overrun was not bad luck on a sound estimate; it was the gap between an inside-view guess and reality, made unrecoverable by an early start.

What the case does not prove

Be careful not to over-learn this case. It does not prove that ambitious buildings should not be built, or that public projects are always mismanaged, or that architects cannot be trusted with budgets. The building has since been listed as a World Heritage site, and many would argue it was worth every dollar to the city that owns it. What the case proves is narrower and more useful to a developer: a budget and a date set before the design exists are guesses, and a project that starts building on a guess has given away its ability to stop. A private developer does not have a state lottery behind him. He has a lender with covenants and an equity account with a bottom. For him, the narrow lesson is the whole lesson.

Applied examples at your scale

This is a composite example. A developer plans a small mixed-use building with an unusual cantilevered upper floor. He uses a cost per square foot from ordinary apartment buildings, because that is the number he has. The cantilever needs a transfer structure that ordinary buildings do not, and the structural design is not finished when he signs the construction contract. The overrun is not a surprise in hindsight; it was built into a reference class that did not match the building.

A second composite. A developer is about to tell a lender that construction takes 14 months. Before he does, he writes beside it the reference-class figure from his records: similar buildings in his market took a middle value of 19. He now has to write one paragraph explaining the five-month gap. He cannot, so he tells the lender 19, and sizes his interest reserve accordingly. Nothing dramatic happened. That is what a working rule looks like.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is the unprecedented project: a building unusual enough that no reference class fits. That is exactly when the inside view feels most necessary and is most dangerous. The control is to widen the reference class to unusual projects in general, which overrun more than ordinary ones, and to carry a much larger contingency, or to resolve the design before committing.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads this story as a lesson about a difficult architect or a hostile minister. People problems were real, but they arrived inside a project that was already financially impossible. Look for the decision that made the people problems expensive.

Callback

In lesson 2, Berlin's owner held a public date it had not earned. Sydney is the same family of failure at an earlier point: the date and the budget were set before the design that would justify them existed. Rule 1 says only written criteria open a gate. Rule 2 adds what those criteria must include: the outside view.

Recap

Sydney's early estimate was about A$7 million and a 1963 opening; it opened on 20 October 1973 at a reported A$102 million. Construction started before the roof could be designed, the estimate had no reference class, and the architect left before completion. A masterpiece and a failed project. Rule 2: before I commit to a cost or a date, I write the reference-class figure beside my own and explain any gap in writing.

Next: Priya, The Money — what optimism costs: delay, carry and the speed of your decisions.
checklist: Separate two questions on every project: is the building good, and does the project succeed?
Write the reference-class figure beside every cost and date you commit to.
Explain any gap between your figure and the reference class in writing before committing.
Do not start construction on any element whose design is unresolved.
For unusual buildings, widen the reference class and carry a larger contingency.
Reset the estimate at a gate whenever it is revised upward twice.
Keep the holder of the design intent engaged through completion, with a clear contract.
head: Field checklist
speak: The Sydney Opera House won its competition in 1957 with an early estimate of about seven million Australian dollars and a target opening in 1963. Construction began in 1959, before anyone knew how to build the roof shells. Estimates rose repeatedly, early work had to be revisited, and after a change of government the architect, Jørn Utzon, resigned in 1966 and left. It opened on 20 October 1973 at a reported cost of about 102 million. The building is a masterpiece; the project failed. The root cause was committing to a cost and a date with no reference class and no resolved design, then starting construction anyway. A low first number gets the yes, and the true number arrives too late to say no. My rule from this case: before I commit to a cost or a date, I write the reference-class figure beside my own and explain any gap in writing.
terms: Planning fallacy — the tendency to underestimate the time, cost and risk of a plan, even when similar projects ran over.
Design intent — the designer's understanding of what the building is meant to be and why, which is lost if they leave early.
Unprecedented project — a project unusual enough that no close reference class exists, which calls for wider classes and larger contingency.

hostile.q: Your design has a feature nobody in this market has built. How can you give me a budget at all?
hostile.a: I give you two numbers. The ordinary part of the building is estimated against a reference class. The unusual element is carried as a separate allowance with its own large contingency, and it has its own gate: the structural design for it is resolved and priced before I commit to construction.

rule: Rule 2: Before I commit to a cost or a date, I write the reference-class figure beside my own estimate and explain any gap in writing.

title: What optimism costs: delay, carry and the speed of your decisions
summary: Every month of delay costs interest, holding costs and return, and it eats the loan's interest reserve. On a hypothetical project a six-month delay removes about $600,000 of profit and drops the equity's annual return from about 12 percent to about 7 percent. The cheapest defence is fast, well-made decisions.
body:
Delay is never free. Every month adds interest, holding costs and lost return on your equity, and it drains the loan's interest reserve. The planning fallacy shows up on the income statement as carry, and the cheapest defence against carry is a faster decision loop.

Recall

Q. In lesson 6, what is the single output of a gate meeting?

A. Go, no-go or not yet, with the reason in writing.

Q. In lesson 3, why do developers usually run out of cash before they run out of profit?

A. Because overruns and delays arrive as cash calls on the equity, often mid-construction, when the lender will not advance more.

Q. In lesson 1, which of the four levers is the developer most able to control?

A. Time.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a lender reads a schedule as a cost. When you say "18 months" and the outside view says 23, the lender hears five months of interest you have not funded. This lesson puts numbers on what optimism costs, so you can see why your schedule estimate matters as much as your cost estimate, and why the speed of your own decisions is one of the few levers fully in your hands.

Carry: the cost of the calendar

In plain English, carrying cost is what it costs just to keep a project alive for another month, whether or not anything gets built. It includes interest on the loan, insurance, property taxes on the land, site security, staff and your consultants' standing costs.

Worked example one. This is hypothetical, and the interest rate is an illustrative commercial figure, not a forecast. A construction loan has an average drawn balance of $9 million during the late stages, at an annual interest rate of 8 percent. Other holding costs run to $40,000 a month. The project runs six months late.

  1. Interest: $9,000,000 times 8 percent times 6 divided by 12 equals $360,000.
  2. Other holding costs: $40,000 times 6 equals $240,000.
  3. Total carry from the delay: $600,000.

On the hypothetical $2 million profit we have used since lesson 1, six months of delay has removed 30 percent of it, without a single extra brick. That is before counting any rise in construction cost caused by the same delay, or the risk that the market's multiple has moved by the time you sell.

The return on your equity falls twice

Delay hurts your equity in two ways at once: there is less profit, and it arrives later. The internal rate of return (IRR) captures both. In plain English, IRR is the annual growth rate that your money effectively earned, taking timing into account. When there is a single investment in and a single payment out, it is simply the yearly rate that turns one into the other.

Worked example two, hypothetical. You invest $5 million of equity and receive $7 million back after three years.

  • The money grows by a factor of 7 divided by 5, which is 1.4, over three years. The annual rate that compounds to 1.4 in three years is about 11.9 percent. That is the IRR.
  • Now the six-month delay: $600,000 less profit, so $6.4 million back, after three and a half years. The factor is 1.28 over 3.5 years. The annual rate is about 7.3 percent.

Profit fell by 30 percent; the annual return fell by about 40 percent. Time is in the denominator of every return you will ever quote, so a delay hurts more than its dollar cost suggests.

Say that out loud now.

The interest reserve runs dry

Most construction loans include an interest reserve: an amount inside the loan budget set aside to pay the loan's own interest during construction, because the building earns nothing yet. It is sized for the planned schedule. When the project runs late, the reserve runs out before the building is finished, and the lender commonly requires the owner to deposit fresh equity to keep the loan's budget balanced. That is a commercial practice set by each loan agreement, not a rule of law; read your own agreement. You will study it properly in week 40. For now, notice the chain: an optimistic schedule leads to an undersized interest reserve, which leads to a cash call at the worst moment, which is exactly the equity exhaustion Sage warned about in lesson 3.

Delay and the fourth lever

There is a cost of delay that never appears in the carry calculation: the market moves while you wait. In lesson 1, a fall in the market's multiple from 16 to 14 wiped out the hypothetical profit on its own. A project planned to finish in a strong market can finish, six months later, in a weaker one. You cannot forecast the multiple, but you can recognise that delay increases your exposure to it, because it lengthens the period in which a change can catch you before you have sold or refinanced.

A simple applied check: run the pro forma with the delay and with a multiple one turn lower, at the same time. On our hypothetical building, that is $600,000 of carry plus a $1 million fall in value, from $16 million to $15 million. The combined effect removes $1.6 million of a $2 million profit. Delay and a softer market are not independent events; long projects are more likely to meet a turn in the cycle, which Remi will cover in week 27.

Speed of decision: the OODA loop

You cannot control the weather or the permit office. You can control how long your own decisions take. The OODA loop, developed by the American military strategist John Boyd, describes any decision cycle as four steps: observe what is happening, orient by interpreting it against what you know, decide, and act. Boyd's point was that the side that cycles through the loop faster and more accurately gains the advantage.

On a building site, a problem turns up every week: a clash between ducts and beams, a late delivery, a question from the inspector. Each one waits for an owner's decision. Using the carry in example one, $600,000 over six months is about $23,000 a week. A decision that waits three weeks for the next scheduled meeting can cost about $70,000 of carry if it holds up the critical work, before counting its effect on anything else. A decision made in three days costs a fraction of that.

The professional habit is to pre-authorise. Decide in advance which decisions your project manager can make alone and up to what value, which need you within 48 hours, and which need a gate. Speed comes from preparation, not from rushing.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a schedule built from the inside view and financed as if it were certain. The control is to size the loan term and the interest reserve on the reference-class schedule, not on your plan, and to negotiate an extension option before you need it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner confuses fast with hasty. He makes quick decisions without orientation, and pays for them in rework. Boyd's loop puts orientation, the interpretation step, at its centre. Fast and well oriented beats fast and wrong, and both beat slow.

Callback

In lesson 1, Remi called time the lever you control most, because most delay begins with a decision that was not made. This lesson puts a weekly price on that sentence. Every unmade decision on the critical path has a carrying cost, and you can now calculate it.

Recap

Carry is the cost of the calendar: interest plus holding costs, about $600,000 for six months in our hypothetical example. Delay cuts both profit and IRR, and IRR falls faster because time is in its denominator. An optimistic schedule undersizes the interest reserve and triggers a cash call. The OODA loop, with pre-authorised decisions, is how you keep your own decisions off the critical path.

Next: Omar, The Rules — the decision on the record: duty of care, business judgment and the decision journal.
checklist: Calculate the monthly carrying cost of the project: interest plus every holding cost.
Convert it to a weekly figure and keep it visible to the whole team.
Size the loan term and interest reserve on the reference-class schedule, not your plan.
Negotiate an extension option before you need it.
Quote IRR alongside profit so that the cost of time is visible.
Write a decision authority table: what the project manager decides alone, what needs you within 48 hours, what needs a gate.
Track how many days each owner decision took.
head: Field checklist
speak: Delay is never free. Carrying cost is interest plus holding costs, the price of keeping a project alive another month. On a hypothetical loan averaging nine million at eight percent, plus forty thousand a month of holding costs, a six-month delay costs about six hundred thousand dollars, thirty percent of a two million profit, without a brick laid. My return falls twice: less profit, later. Five million in, seven million out after three years is about a twelve percent IRR. With the delay, 6.4 million after three and a half years, it is about seven percent. An optimistic schedule also undersizes the interest reserve, which runs out and becomes a cash call. What I control is the speed of my own decisions. Boyd's OODA loop: observe, orient, decide, act. I pre-authorise decisions so none waits three weeks for a meeting, because on this project each week costs about twenty-three thousand.
terms: Carrying cost — what it costs to keep a project alive for a period, chiefly interest and holding costs, whether or not work progresses.
Internal rate of return (IRR) — the annual growth rate your money effectively earned, taking the timing of every payment into account.
OODA loop — John Boyd's decision cycle of observe, orient, decide and act; cycling faster and more accurately confers an advantage.

hostile.q: Your interest reserve covers eighteen months of construction. What happens in month nineteen?
hostile.a: It does not cover eighteen. I sized the reserve on my reference-class schedule of 24 months, which is longer than my own plan, and I have negotiated a six-month extension option. If both are exceeded, the equity top-up comes from the liquidity reserve identified in my plan, which I can show you.

title: The decision on the record: duty of care, business judgment and the decision journal
summary: People who make decisions for a company generally owe it a duty of care, and in many legal systems courts are reluctant to second-guess an informed, good-faith, unconflicted business decision. What protects you is the process: evidence considered, conflicts declared, and a record. A decision journal builds the habit, with care about what you write.
body:
A bad outcome is not proof of a bad decision, but only if you can show how the decision was made. The law in many places generally protects informed, good-faith, unconflicted business judgment, and the record is how you show it. A decision journal builds the habit, provided you write it with care.

Recall

Q. In lesson 7's Red Pen memo, why was "we have already spent $180,000" a defect?

A. Because it is sunk cost, which Rule 1 says cannot move you past a gate.

Q. In lesson 1, why must gate criteria be written before the spend?

A. Because after the spend, judgment is contaminated by sunk cost and by wanting your work to matter.

Q. In lesson 3, what is committed cost?

A. Money you are legally obliged to spend, whether or not it has been paid yet.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will make decisions for companies that hold land and borrow money, and later for companies in which other people have invested. Some decisions will turn out badly. When that happens, a partner, an investor, a lender or a liquidator may ask whether you did your job properly. The answer will depend less on the outcome than on how the decision was made and what record exists. This lesson teaches the concepts. The specific duties, standards and protections depend on the jurisdiction and the type of entity, so verify them against the primary source before you rely on them. Professional sign-off required: corporate lawyer.

The duty of care

In plain English: if you make decisions for a company, you are expected to take reasonable care, which means getting the information a careful person would get, thinking about it, and acting honestly in the company's interest.

The professional framing: directors and officers of a company commonly owe it duties, usually described as a duty of care, which concerns the diligence and skill of decision-making, and a duty of loyalty or good faith, which concerns acting in the company's interest rather than your own. How these duties are defined, to whom they are owed, and what standard of care applies differ between legal systems and are set out in statutes and case law you must check for your own situation.

The business judgment idea

Courts in a number of common-law jurisdictions show a form of deference to business decisions. The idea, often called the business judgment rule, is that a court will not substitute its own hindsight for a decision-maker's judgment if the decision was made on an informed basis, in good faith, without a conflict of interest, and within a range of reasonable choices. The precise test, and whether it exists at all in a particular place, varies; verify it against the primary source before you rely on it.

What matters for you is the shape of the idea, because it tells you what a defensible decision looks like. It is not about being right. It is about being informed, unconflicted, honest and reasonable, and being able to show it.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example one: the bad outcome, well made

This is hypothetical. A company you direct buys a site after a gate review. The record shows: a soil report, a cost estimate, a reference-class check on schedule, a lender's indicative terms, the gate criteria signed beforehand, and a short note of the discussion including one adviser's dissent and why you proceeded. A year later, interest rates rise sharply, the market's multiple falls, and the project is shelved at a loss.

The decision lost money, but the record shows an informed, good-faith process with the dissent considered. That is the kind of decision the business judgment idea is designed to protect. The investor may still be unhappy, but the argument that you were careless has little to stand on.

Worked example two: the good outcome, badly made

Same company, a different site. You approve a construction contract with a builder in which your brother-in-law holds a share. You do not mention it. There is no competitive bid and no written analysis. The project goes well and makes money.

The outcome was good, and the decision is still exposed: an undeclared conflict of interest, meaning a situation where your personal interest could influence your duty to the company, combined with no record of why this builder was chosen. Deference of the business-judgment kind generally depends on the absence of a conflict, so in this situation it may not help you at all. The professional move would have been to declare the interest in writing, step out of the decision, obtain competing bids, and have the decision made and recorded by someone without the conflict.

The decision journal, and how to write it

A decision journal is a personal practice: for every significant decision, you write down, at the time, what you decided, the options you considered, what you knew, what you expected to happen with rough probabilities, and what would make you change your mind. Its main purpose is learning. Months later you compare what you expected with what happened, which is the only reliable way to discover whether your judgment is calibrated or just lucky.

It also happens to build exactly the habits the law rewards: informed decisions and a contemporaneous record. But be careful. Notes you write about company business may be disclosable to the other side if there is ever a dispute, and casual words can be read very differently later. Write facts, reasoning and expectations, not jokes, insults or speculation about people's motives. Keep legal advice in separate, properly labelled communications with your lawyer. Ask your lawyer how your journal should be kept. Vera will cover records and privilege properly in week 82.

What a decision record should contain

A business record of a significant decision does not need to be long. A useful minimum is:

  • The date, the decision-makers present, and the decision itself, stated in one sentence.
  • The information relied on, listed by name: reports, estimates, legal advice obtained, lender terms.
  • The options considered, including doing nothing.
  • Any interest declared, and who stepped out as a result.
  • Any dissent, and why the decision went the other way.
  • The conditions or next gate attached to the decision.

For a company, this record usually lives in board or management minutes, kept in the minute book. Omar will return to minute books and resolutions in week 35. The point now is that the record should be created at the time, not reconstructed afterwards, and it should be complete enough that a stranger could see what you knew and why you chose as you did.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an undeclared conflict, because it can remove the protection that a careful process would otherwise earn. The control is a standing conflicts register: every relationship you or your close family have with any counterparty, declared in writing before any decision touching it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner keeps no record because he trusts himself and he is busy. Then, two years later, he cannot remember why he did what he did, and neither can anyone else. Memory is not a record. Five lines written on the day are worth more than an hour of recollection in a lawyer's office.

Callback

In lesson 6, Remi ended the gate meeting with a gate note: each criterion, the evidence and the decision, signed. That note is the business record this lesson is about. The gate process you are learning is not only good management; it is also the shape of a defensible decision.

Recap

Decision-makers generally owe a duty of care and a duty of loyalty. Many courts defer to informed, good-faith, unconflicted business judgment, though the test varies and must be verified. Protection comes from process: evidence, declared conflicts and a record. Keep a decision journal for learning, write it carefully, and ask your lawyer how to keep it.

Next: Quincy, The Numbers — working backward from the margin you need to the estimate you can afford.
checklist: Keep a conflicts register and declare any interest in writing before the decision it touches.
Step out of any decision where you have a conflict, and have it decided and recorded by someone else.
Record each significant decision: options, evidence, dissent and reasons.
Keep a decision journal of expectations and probabilities, and review it against outcomes.
Write facts and reasoning; never jokes, insults or speculation about motives.
Keep legal advice in separate, labelled communications with your lawyer.
Ask a corporate lawyer which duties apply to your role and entity in your jurisdiction.
head: Field checklist
speak: A bad outcome is not proof of a bad decision, but only if I can show how I decided. People who make decisions for a company generally owe it a duty of care and a duty of loyalty. In many common-law places, courts show deference to business judgment that was informed, in good faith, unconflicted and reasonable, though the exact test varies and I verify it for my own situation. So a well-documented decision that loses money because rates rose is defensible, while a profitable decision with an undeclared conflict and no record is exposed. My controls are a conflicts register, declarations before decisions, and a short record of evidence, dissent and reasons. I also keep a decision journal, mainly to learn whether my judgment is calibrated. I write facts and reasoning, not opinions about people, and I ask my lawyer how to keep it.
terms: Duty of care — the obligation of a company's decision-makers to act with the diligence and skill a careful person would use.
Business judgment rule — the idea, applied in various forms by some courts, that informed, good-faith, unconflicted business decisions should not be second-guessed with hindsight.
Conflict of interest — a situation in which your personal interest could influence your duty to the company.

hostile.q: From an investor's lawyer: the project lost money. Why should we not hold you personally responsible?
hostile.a: Because the decision was made through a documented process: the gate criteria set beforehand, the studies, the lender's terms, the dissent considered and recorded, and no conflict on my part. I will provide the gate note and the supporting reports. The loss came from a rise in rates that was disclosed as a risk at the time.

title: Working backward from the margin: how much estimate can you afford?
summary: Start from the finished outcome you need and work backward. On a hypothetical $16 million building that must earn 15 percent on cost, all-in cost can be at most $13.91 million; a reference-class uplift of 18 percent at the confidence you choose then caps your base estimate at $11.79 million. The same method sets the longest schedule a loan term can carry.
body:
Instead of asking whether your estimate produces enough profit, start from the profit you need and work backward to the largest estimate you can afford, after the reference class has had its say. If your estimate is bigger than that, the project fails the gate before anyone argues about details.

Recall

Q. In lesson 8, what are the three steps of reference class forecasting?

A. Choose a class of similar projects, find the distribution of their outcomes, and place your project in it, adjusting only for evidenced differences.

Q. In lesson 3, how much cost overrun eats the whole profit?

A. An overrun equal to the profit on cost; at 14.3 percent profit on cost, about a 14.3 percent overrun.

Q. In lesson 5, what does a study's value depend on?

A. The probability of the problem, the size of the loss it avoids, and whether its result could change your decision.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a forward calculation, cost plus profit equals value, invites you to tweak the inputs until the answer looks good. A reverse calculation fixes the answer first: the value the market will pay and the return you require. Then it tells you the most you can spend. This is how disciplined developers and lenders actually test a deal, and it turns Rule 2 into arithmetic.

Two terms first

A percentile describes a position in a distribution. P50 is the middle outcome: half of comparable projects did better, half did worse. P80 is the outcome that 80 percent of projects did better than and 20 percent did worse than. Choosing P80 means you plan for a bad-but-not-unusual result. An uplift is the percentage you add to your base estimate to move it to a chosen percentile of the reference class.

Worked example one: the most you can afford to estimate

This is hypothetical. All figures are round numbers for teaching, and the 15 percent hurdle is a commercial choice you would set, not a standard.

Step 1. Fix the outcome. The completed building is valued at $16,000,000: net operating income of $1,000,000 a year times a multiple of 16. You require profit on cost of at least 15 percent.

Step 2. Find the maximum all-in cost. If profit on cost is 15 percent, value equals cost times 1.15. So the maximum cost is $16,000,000 divided by 1.15, which equals $13,913,000, rounded to the nearest thousand dollars.

Step 3. Bring in the reference class. Suppose your class of 20 comparable projects shows cost overruns from budget at the same design stage of 8 percent at P50 and 18 percent at P80. You decide, as a matter of judgment, to plan at P80.

Step 4. Find the maximum base estimate. Your base estimate times 1.18 must not exceed $13,913,000. So the base estimate must not exceed $13,913,000 divided by 1.18, which equals $11,791,000.

Step 5. Compare. Your cost consultant's base estimate is $12,500,000. That is $709,000 above the maximum. At P80, the project fails the hurdle.

Say that out loud now.

Reading the gap

Now you have a precise problem instead of a vague worry. There are three ways to close a $709,000 gap, and each is a different decision.

  • Cut cost. Find $709,000 of genuine scope reduction, priced by the cost consultant, not hoped for by the architect.
  • Raise value. To carry the $12,500,000 estimate at P80, value must be $12,500,000 times 1.18 times 1.15, which equals $16,962,500, about 6 percent higher. At a multiple of 16, net operating income must rise from $1,000,000 to about $1,060,000 a year. Is there real evidence for 6 percent higher rents, or is that the inside view talking?
  • Accept less confidence. At P50 the maximum base estimate is $13,913,000 divided by 1.08, which equals $12,882,000. Your $12,500,000 passes. But you are now accepting roughly a one-in-two chance of falling short of your hurdle.

The third option is the dangerous one, because it makes the problem disappear by changing a single assumption. That is legitimate only if you decide it consciously, write it in the gate note, and size your equity reserve for the P80 case anyway.

Check it forward

Always check a reverse calculation by running it forward. Take the maximum base estimate of $11,791,000. Multiply by 1.18 to get the P80 cost: $13,913,000. Multiply by 1.15 to get the value needed: $16,000,000. The arithmetic closes, so the reverse steps were right. This takes thirty seconds and catches the most common error, dividing where you should have multiplied.

Now apply the beginner's-mistake correction below with numbers. Suppose the land in the estimate is $2,500,000 and already fixed by contract. Only the remaining costs can overrun. Maximum all-in cost is still $13,913,000. Subtract the fixed land: $11,413,000 is the most the variable costs can reach at P80. Divide by 1.18: the variable base estimate can be at most $9,672,000. Add back the land: a total base estimate of $12,172,000. Separating fixed from variable costs has given you $381,000 more room, and it is more honest, because land you have already priced does not overrun.

Worked example two: the longest schedule a loan can carry

The same reverse method works for time. Hypothetical again. A lender offers a construction loan with a term of 30 months, and you cannot rely on an extension. Your reference class shows schedule overruns of 25 percent at P80.

  1. Fix the outcome: construction must finish within 30 months.
  2. Reverse the uplift: 30 months divided by 1.25 equals 24 months.
  3. Your base schedule must therefore be no more than 24 months.

If your contractor's programme is 26 months, then at P80 you will run to about 32.5 months, 2.5 months past the loan. You now know exactly what to ask the lender for: a longer term or an extension option of at least three months, before you sign, not when month 30 arrives.

Notice what the reverse method did to the conversation. Without it, the lender asks whether 26 months is realistic and you both offer opinions. With it, you arrive saying: "Our reference class implies about 32.5 months at P80; your term is 30; here is the extension we need." That is a request backed by evidence, and lenders respond to evidence far better than to confidence. The same is true of your own gate: a number derived backward from a requirement is much harder to talk yourself out of than a number you adjusted until it felt right.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing the percentile after you see the answer. If P80 fails and P50 passes, the temptation is to discover that P50 was always the right choice. The control is to write the chosen percentile into the gate criteria before the estimate arrives, alongside the hurdle.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner applies the uplift to the whole budget, including land he has already bought at a fixed price. The uplift belongs to the uncertain parts of cost, mainly construction and soft costs. In this example we applied it to the whole base estimate for simplicity; in practice you would separate land and other fixed amounts from the costs that can still move, and apply the reference-class uplift to the costs that genuinely vary.

Callback

In lesson 3, Sage taught that profit on cost tells you how much cost can rise before profit is gone. This lesson runs that idea in reverse: fix the profit you need, fix the confidence you want, and the arithmetic tells you how much cost you can afford to estimate.

Recap

Work backward: value divided by one plus the hurdle gives the maximum all-in cost; that divided by one plus the reference-class uplift gives the maximum base estimate. Here, $16 million at 15 percent and P80 allows $11.79 million against an estimate of $12.5 million, a gap of $709,000. The same method caps the schedule a loan can carry. Fix the percentile before the estimate arrives.

Next: Kema, The Room — running the pre-mortem and the after-action review.
checklist: Fix the completed value and the required hurdle before reviewing the estimate.
Compute the maximum all-in cost: value divided by one plus the hurdle.
Write the planning percentile into the gate criteria before the estimate arrives.
Divide by one plus the reference-class uplift to get the maximum base estimate.
Apply the uplift only to costs that can still move, not to land already fixed.
Reverse the schedule too: loan term divided by one plus the schedule uplift.
State the gap in dollars and months, and name which of the three remedies you choose.
head: Field checklist
speak: I work backward from the outcome I need. On a hypothetical building worth sixteen million, if I require fifteen percent profit on cost, the most I can spend all-in is sixteen million divided by 1.15, about 13.91 million. My reference class shows overruns of eight percent at the middle and eighteen percent at P80, the bad-but-not-unusual case. Planning at P80, my base estimate can be no more than 13.91 million divided by 1.18, about 11.79 million. The estimate is 12.5 million, so the gap is about 709 thousand. I can cut that much real scope, find evidence for about six percent more value, or consciously accept P50, which means roughly even odds of missing my hurdle. The same method works for time: a thirty-month loan with a twenty-five percent schedule uplift allows a base schedule of twenty-four months. And I fix the percentile before the estimate arrives.
terms: Percentile (P50, P80) — the outcome that 50 or 80 percent of comparable projects did better than; P80 is a bad-but-not-unusual case.
Uplift — the percentage added to a base estimate to move it to a chosen percentile of the reference class.
Hurdle — the minimum return or margin you require before a project passes a gate; a commercial choice, not a standard.

hostile.q: Your base estimate is twelve and a half million. Your own reverse calculation says the maximum is eleven point eight. Why are you still here?
hostile.a: Because the gate has not passed and I am not asking you to fund it yet. I have three paths: $709,000 of priced scope reduction, which the cost consultant is testing now; evidence for higher rents, which I do not yet have; or a lower confidence level, which I will not adopt. If the first path fails, the project does not proceed.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Running the pre-mortem and the after-action review
summary: A pre-mortem asks your team to imagine the project has already failed and explain why, which surfaces risks that ordinary meetings bury. Inversion asks what would guarantee failure. An after-action review closes the loop with four questions after the event. You run all three without defending your plan.
body:
Before a big commitment, run a pre-mortem: tell the team the project has already failed and ask them why. After an event, run an after-action review: what was supposed to happen, what did, why, and what we will do next time. Your job in both rooms is to invite bad news and not defend yourself.

Recall

Q. In lesson 9, what was the root cause at the Sydney Opera House?

A. Committing to a cost and a date with no reference class and no resolved design, then starting construction anyway.

Q. In lesson 6, what should you do after asking for a number in a gate meeting?

A. Stay silent and let the answer arrive.

Q. In lesson 2, what does the seven-step forensic method refuse to do until late?

A. Name the root cause; it looks at decisions, assumptions and incentives first.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, in an ordinary meeting, people do not volunteer the reasons your project might fail. They are polite, they want the work, and you are the client. Asking "any concerns?" usually produces silence. The pre-mortem is a structured way to make raising risks the expected, even rewarded, thing to do. The after-action review does the same after the event, so that your team and you actually learn instead of assigning blame.

The pre-mortem

In plain English: you ask people to imagine it is the future and the project has failed badly, then to write down why. The research psychologist Gary Klein described the method in a 2007 article in the Harvard Business Review. Imagining that failure has already happened changes the question from "could this go wrong?", which people resist, to "explain why it went wrong", which people are surprisingly good at.

The scene. This is a composite example. Two weeks before you close on land for a hypothetical 40-unit building, you gather the architect, cost consultant, project manager and lawyer for 45 minutes.

  1. You say: "It is two years from now. This project has been a disaster. Take three minutes, on your own, and write down every reason it failed."
  2. Silence while they write. Do not fill it.
  3. Go round the table, one reason per person per round, until the reasons run out. Write each on a board without comment.
  4. Group them, then pick the three most likely or most damaging. For each, assign an owner and one action before the gate.

Worked example one. The reasons come back: the soil was worse than the desk study suggested; the electrical utility took nine months to provide service; a neighbour appealed the approval; the lead framer went out of business. The utility point is new to you. The project manager knew from another job that service upgrades in this area are slow. In a normal meeting, nobody asked. Now it gets an owner and an action: a written request to the utility for a service timeline before closing.

Say that out loud now.

Inversion

Inversion is the same idea applied to your own thinking: instead of asking how to succeed, ask what would guarantee failure, then avoid those things. The advice to invert is usually traced to the nineteenth-century mathematician Carl Jacobi, and it was popularised among investors by Charlie Munger.

Applied example: "How would I guarantee this project runs out of money?" Answers come quickly: size the interest reserve on my own schedule; fund overruns from hope; sign the construction contract before the design is complete; hire the cheapest builder without checking their finances. Each answer is a control written in reverse. Inversion is useful alone, at your desk, before the pre-mortem, so that you arrive having already done the uncomfortable thinking yourself.

The after-action review

An after-action review is a short structured debrief after an event, developed by the United States Army. It asks four questions:

  1. What was supposed to happen?
  2. What actually happened?
  3. Why was there a difference?
  4. What will we do differently next time, and what will we keep?

Worked example two, a composite. A concrete pour was delayed a day because the inspection was not booked. The review takes 15 minutes on site. Supposed to happen: pour Tuesday after inspection. Actually happened: inspector not booked, pour moved to Wednesday, crew paid to wait. Why: the inspection booking was nobody's named task. Next time: every required inspection is a named line in the look-ahead schedule with a person responsible. Keep: the crew's early arrival, which let the pour finish on Wednesday morning.

The rule of the room is that the review is about the system, not about punishing a person. If people expect blame, they will hide facts, and you will learn nothing. That does not mean nobody is accountable; it means accountability is handled separately from learning.

The lines to say and never to say

  • Say: "Thank you. That is exactly the kind of thing I need to hear."
  • Say: "What did we know at the time, and when did we know it?"
  • Never say: "That will not happen here."
  • Never say, in a review: "Whose fault was this?"

A further line worth having ready: "If you were in my seat, which of these would you fix first?" It moves the consultant from critic to adviser and usually produces the most practical answer of the meeting.

The question behind the question: when a consultant raises a risk tentatively, the question behind it is often "Is it safe to tell you this?" Your response to the first bad news decides whether you get the second. Hold your state by thanking them and writing it down before you react.

When to stay silent

Stay silent at three moments. First, during the writing time; even a helpful comment from you resets everyone's list toward yours. Second, after a reason is offered, until it is written on the board; any response from you, even agreement, starts a discussion that stops the round. Third, when someone pauses mid-sentence after a hard point. That pause is often the person deciding whether to say the next, harder thing. Let them decide in your favour.

Holding your state

Hearing six people describe how your project fails is uncomfortable, especially if you have put money and reputation into it. You will feel the urge to explain why each risk is handled. Resist it in the room; the explanation can come later, in writing, against each owner's action. A practical habit is to keep a pen moving: writing every point down gives your hands something to do, slows your reaction, and shows the team that their point has been taken seriously. When the meeting ends, read the top three risks back aloud with their owners and dates, thank everyone, and close. The tone you set in the first pre-mortem decides how honest the second one will be.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is running a pre-mortem as theatre: you listen, nod, and change nothing. The control is to leave with the three top risks, each with an owner, an action and a deadline, recorded in the gate file.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner speaks first and states his own view of the risks. After that, everyone else's list shrinks to match the boss's. Make people write alone before anyone speaks, and speak last yourself.

Callback

In lesson 2, Ford traced Berlin's failure through warning signs that were ordinary and visible. A pre-mortem is the cheapest known way to surface such signs before the commitment, and an after-action review is how a team stops repeating them.

Recap

The pre-mortem asks the team to explain a failure that has not happened yet; write alone first, go round the table, assign owners. Inversion asks what would guarantee failure. The after-action review asks four questions after the event and focuses on the system, not on blame. Speak last, thank bad news, and leave with actions.

Next: Kema, Quiz and Recap — week 2, judgment.
checklist: Before every major commitment, run a 45-minute pre-mortem with the core team.
Make everyone write reasons alone before anyone speaks; speak last yourself.
Leave with the top three risks, each with an owner, an action and a deadline.
Invert alone first: list what would guarantee failure, and turn each into a control.
After every significant event, run a 15-minute after-action review with the four questions.
Keep reviews about the system; handle accountability separately.
Thank whoever brings bad news, and write it down before reacting.
head: Field checklist
speak: Before a big commitment I run a pre-mortem. I tell the team: it is two years from now and this project failed badly; take three minutes and write down why. Everyone writes alone, then we go round the table, one reason each, until they run out. We pick the three most dangerous, and each gets an owner and an action before the gate. Imagining failure as a fact makes people far more willing to name risks than asking if anyone has concerns. On my own I invert: what would guarantee this project runs out of money? Every answer becomes a control. After an event I run an after-action review: what was supposed to happen, what happened, why the difference, and what we change and keep. It is about the system, not blame. I speak last, I thank bad news, and I leave with actions.
terms: Pre-mortem — a meeting that asks people to imagine a project has already failed and explain why, to surface risks before commitment.
Inversion — reasoning about how to guarantee failure, then avoiding those causes.
After-action review — a short structured debrief asking what was supposed to happen, what happened, why, and what to change.

hostile.q: From your architect: a pre-mortem two weeks before closing? It sounds like you are losing confidence in the project.
hostile.a: The opposite. I am confident enough to look for the reasons it could fail while they are still cheap to fix. I will close with more confidence afterwards, not less, and the risks we find will each have an owner.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 2 quiz and recap: judgment
summary: Six questions test the week: the outside view, Sydney, carry and IRR, the duty of care and the business judgment idea, reverse-engineering the estimate, and the pre-mortem and after-action review. A Red Pen drill and a two-minute boardroom drill put them to use.
body:
This week was about judgment: where your forecasts come from, what optimism costs, how a defensible decision is made and recorded, and how a team surfaces risks before and after the event. Now you produce it from memory.

Recall

Q. In lesson 10, what did a six-month delay cost on the hypothetical project?

A. About $600,000 of carry, and the equity's IRR fell from about 11.9 percent to about 7.3 percent.

Q. In lesson 1, what are the four levers?

A. Income, cost, time and the market's multiple.

Q. In lesson 11, what can remove the protection a careful process would otherwise earn?

A. An undeclared conflict of interest.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, judgment is not a talent you either have or lack. It is a set of habits: start from the outside view, price time, keep a record, and invite bad news. Habits only form through use. Answer each question aloud, then check yourself. Mark any you hesitated on. The questions mix the qualitative and the arithmetic deliberately, because in a real meeting you will need to switch between explaining a principle and running a number without pausing.

The six questions

Question 1. What is the difference between the inside view and the outside view, and which comes first?

Answer: The inside view builds an estimate from the details of your own plan; the outside view starts from what actually happened on a reference class of similar projects. The outside view comes first; then you adjust only for differences you can evidence.

Question 2. What was the root cause at the Sydney Opera House, and what is Rule 2?

Answer: Committing to a cost and a date with no reference class and no resolved design, then starting construction anyway. Rule 2: before I commit to a cost or a date, I write the reference-class figure beside my own and explain any gap in writing.

Question 3. Why does a delay hurt IRR more than it hurts profit?

Answer: Because a delay reduces profit through carry and also pushes the return later, and time is in the denominator of every annual return. In the lesson 10 example, profit fell 30 percent and IRR fell about 40 percent.

Question 4. What makes a business decision defensible under the business judgment idea, in general terms?

Answer: It was informed, made in good faith, free of undeclared conflicts, within a range of reasonable choices, and recorded. The precise test varies by jurisdiction and must be verified against the primary source.

Question 5. A building will be worth $20 million and you require 20 percent profit on cost. Your reference class shows a P80 overrun of 15 percent. What is the most your base estimate can be?

Answer: Maximum all-in cost is $20 million divided by 1.2, which is $16,667,000. Divided by 1.15, the maximum base estimate is about $14,493,000.

Question 6. Name the four questions of an after-action review.

Answer: What was supposed to happen? What actually happened? Why was there a difference? What will we do differently next time, and what will we keep?

Say that out loud now.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical schedule note to a lender and find the defects before reading on.

Construction will take 16 months; our contractor is very good. The interest reserve is sized for 16 months. We considered similar buildings but ours is simpler, so they are not relevant. We plan at P50, which we chose after seeing that P80 did not meet our hurdle. There were no significant risks raised at the team meeting, where I opened by explaining why I think the schedule is achievable. The general contractor is a company in which my business partner has an interest.

The defects:

  1. "Our contractor is very good" is not evidence for a shorter schedule; every owner says it.
  2. The interest reserve is sized on the inside-view schedule, not the reference class, and there is no extension option.
  3. Dismissing the reference class because "ours is simpler" without written evidence breaks Rule 2.
  4. Choosing the percentile after seeing that P80 failed is exactly the risk lesson 12 warned about.
  5. "No significant risks were raised" after the owner spoke first is predictable silence, not evidence of safety.
  6. The partner's interest in the contractor is a conflict of interest that should have been declared and handled before the decision, with the contractor selection recorded.

Boardroom drill

Two minutes, aloud, to an imaginary investment committee. Then compare.

"Judgment is a set of habits, and this week built four. First, I start every estimate from the outside view: a reference class of similar projects. If my plan says 18 months and twelve similar buildings took a middle value of 23, I explain the gap in writing or I use 23. That is Rule 2, from the Sydney Opera House, which opened ten years late at many times its early estimate because it was committed before the design existed. Second, I price time: on a hypothetical project, six months of delay costs about 600 thousand and cuts the equity's annual return from about 12 percent to about 7. Third, I keep a record: informed, unconflicted decisions with the reasoning written down are the decisions the law tends to protect. Fourth, I invite bad news, with a pre-mortem before commitments and an after-action review after events, and I work backward from the return I need to the most I can afford to estimate."

How to score yourself

One point for each question answered aloud and correctly before you read the answer, and one point for each Red Pen defect you found unaided. There are six defects, so the total is twelve. If you scored nine or below, reread lessons 8 and 12, which carry the method the others rely on. If you got Question 5 wrong, rework it with different numbers until the steps feel automatic: value divided by one plus the hurdle, then divided by one plus the uplift, then checked forward.

For the boardroom drill, record yourself on your phone and listen once. Check three things only. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you give at least one number correctly? Did you end on a rule rather than trailing off? Next week adds the psychology that explains why these habits are hard to keep, so mark anything that felt unnatural to say. That discomfort is usually where the bias lives.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that these habits feel like extra work on a busy week, so they are the first to be skipped. The control is to put them into the gate criteria themselves: no gate passes without a reference-class figure, a pre-mortem record and a written decision note.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner also treats the six questions as separate facts. They are one system. The outside view supplies the probabilities, the reverse calculation turns them into a maximum estimate, carry prices the schedule, the pre-mortem finds what the class missed, and the record makes the decision defensible.

The beginner learns the vocabulary and stops there. Knowing the words "reference class" is worth nothing until you have actually built one. This week, start a spreadsheet with five comparable buildings in your market, planned and actual, even if some cells are blank.

Callback

In lesson 5, Roman priced the value of information. Every tool this week is information bought cheaply: a reference class costs some phone calls, a pre-mortem costs 45 minutes, a decision note costs five lines. Measured against the losses they help avoid, they are the highest-value studies you will ever commission.

Recap

Start from the outside view. Write the reference-class figure beside your own. Price delay as carry and as lost IRR. Make decisions informed, unconflicted and recorded. Work backward from the return you need. Run pre-mortems and after-action reviews and speak last. Rules 1 and 2 now stand together.

head: The six questions
speak: Judgment is a set of habits. I start every estimate from the outside view, a reference class of similar projects, and under Rule 2 I write that figure beside mine and explain any gap. The Sydney Opera House opened ten years late at many times its early estimate because it was committed before the design existed. I price time: on a hypothetical project, six months of delay costs about six hundred thousand and drops the equity return from about twelve percent to about seven. I work backward: value divided by one plus my hurdle, then by one plus the reference-class uplift, gives the most I can afford to estimate. I make decisions informed, unconflicted and recorded, because those are the decisions the law tends to protect. And I invite bad news: a pre-mortem before commitments, an after-action review after events, and I speak last.
terms: Outside view — an estimate that starts from the actual outcomes of similar past projects.
Pre-mortem — a meeting that imagines a project has failed and asks why, before the commitment.
Business judgment rule — the idea, in various forms, that informed, good-faith, unconflicted business decisions are not second-guessed with hindsight.

hostile.q: From a lender: everyone says they use the outside view. Show me yours.
hostile.a: Here is the reference class: the comparable projects, their planned and actual durations and costs, and why each one was included. Here is my estimate beside it, with the one gap I claim and the evidence for it. And here is the loan sizing, which uses the reference-class figures rather than mine.
